3.1.i: 3D problems become 2D problems once you spot the right-angled triangle inside the solid. Volumes of composite shapes are just simple shapes added or removed.
3.1.h: The 3D distance formula is Pythagoras applied twice: once across the base and once up. A cone is one third of the cylinder with the same base and height, as is a pyramid of its prism.
3.1.q: Find the distance between A(1, 2, 3) and B(4, 6, 15), and the midpoint of AB.
s: Differences: 3, 4, 12.
Distance only depends on how far apart the points are in each direction.
Pythagoras in three directions.
Midpoint = (2.5, 4, 9).
The middle of two values is their average, in each coordinate separately.

Distance: (x₁, y₁, z₁) and (x₂, y₂, z₂) are the two points.
For straight-line distance in 3D; drop z for 2D.
Midpoint: The coordinates of the two end points.
For the point exactly halfway along a segment.
Cone and sphere: r radius, h perpendicular height, l slant height.
For cones and spheres. Curved area excludes the circular base of a cone.
Pyramid: A base area, h perpendicular height.
For any pyramid. h must be vertical, not the sloping edge.

3.2.i: Trigonometry links angles and lengths. Right-angled triangles use SOHCAHTOA; for any other triangle, the information you are given decides between the sine rule and the cosine rule.
3.2.h: The cosine rule is Pythagoras with a correction term for when C is not 90°. Since sin θ = sin(180° − θ), finding an angle with the sine rule can give two valid triangles.
3.2.q: In triangle ABC, AB = 8, AC = 5 and angle A = 60°. Find BC and the area.
s: Use the cosine rule: BC² = 64 + 25 − 2(8)(5)cos 60° = 49.
You have two sides and the angle between them, so the sine rule can't start.
BC = 7.
Take the positive root because it is a length.
This formula uses exactly the two sides and included angle you were given.

Sine rule: a, b, c are the sides opposite angles A, B, C.
When you know a side with its opposite angle. Finding an angle may give two answers.
Cosine rule: a, b, c sides, C the angle between a and b.
With two sides and the included angle, or three sides.
Area of a triangle: a, b two sides, C the angle between them.
When the perpendicular height is not known.

3.3.i: These are trigonometry problems told as stories. A clear diagram does most of the work: elevation looks up from horizontal, depression looks down, and bearings are clockwise from north.
3.3.h: Parallel north lines create alternate and co-interior angles, which is how a bearing at one point is carried over to the next. The angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A.
3.3.q: From a point 40 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation of the top is 35°. Find the height of the tower.
s: Draw a right-angled triangle: adjacent 40, angle 35°, height opposite.
The diagram shows which trig ratio connects what you know and want.
Tangent links the opposite and adjacent sides.
Make sure the calculator is in degrees.

3.4.i: An arc is a slice of the circumference and a sector is a slice of the disc. Both are the same fraction of the whole circle: the angle out of 360.
3.4.h: Every measurement in a circle scales with the angle, so the θ/360 fraction applies to both length and area. The perimeter of a sector needs the two radii as well as the arc.
3.4.q: A sector has radius 10 cm and angle 72°. Find the arc length and the area.
s: 72/360 = 1/5 of the circle.
Working out the fraction first keeps the formula simple.
An arc is that fraction of the circumference.
A sector is the same fraction of the area.

Arc length: θ angle in degrees, r radius.
When the angle is in degrees.
Sector area: θ angle in degrees, r radius.
When the angle is in degrees.

3.5.i: The perpendicular bisector of two points is the line of all places equally far from both, like the boundary between two neighbouring shops' areas.
3.5.h: You need two facts: it passes through the midpoint and its gradient is the negative reciprocal of AB's. This is the building block of every Voronoi edge.
3.5.q: Find the perpendicular bisector of A(2, 1) and B(6, 3).
s: Midpoint = (4, 2).
The bisector must pass through the middle of AB.
Gradient of AB = 2/4 = 1/2, so the bisector's gradient is −2.
Perpendicular means the gradients multiply to −1.
A point and a gradient fix the line.

3.6.i: A Voronoi diagram divides a map so that each region contains the places closest to one site, like catchment areas for shops.
3.6.h: A vertex of the diagram is equally far from three sites, so it is where bisectors meet and locally as far as you can get from them. The toxic waste dump problem checks vertices and boundary points and picks the one farthest from its nearest site.
3.6.q: Sites A(0, 0) and B(4, 0) have Voronoi cells separated by which edge? In which cell is P(1, 5)?
s: The edge is the perpendicular bisector: x = 2.
Every Voronoi edge is the bisector between two neighbouring sites.
P has x = 1, which is less than 2, so P is on A's side.
Each cell holds the points closer to its own site.
Check: PA² = 26, PB² = 34.
Comparing squared distances confirms the cell without using square roots.
3.6.a: Edge x = 2; P is in A's cell

3.7.i: A radian measures an angle by arc length: one radian is the angle where the arc equals the radius. That makes circle formulas much simpler.
3.7.h: A full turn has an arc of 2πr, which is 2π radius lengths, so 2π radians equals 360°. Calculus results such as d/dx sin x = cos x only hold in radians.
3.7.q: A sector has radius 6 cm and angle 1.2 radians. Find its arc length and area.
s: With radians the arc is just radius times angle.
The same angle gives the area directly, without a fraction of 360.

Arc and sector (radians): r radius, θ angle in radians, l arc length, A sector area.
Only when θ is in radians. Convert from degrees by × π/180.

3.8.i: On a circle of radius 1, an angle gives a point: its x-coordinate is the cosine, its y-coordinate is the sine. Going round again repeats the values, so trig equations have several solutions.
3.8.h: The Pythagorean identity is Pythagoras on the unit circle. Symmetry in the circle gives the extra solutions: sin θ = sin(π − θ) and cos θ = cos(−θ); then add whole periods to stay in the interval.
s: sin x = 0.5.
Isolate the trig function first.
This is the principal solution.
Also x = π − π/6 = 5π/6.
Sine is also positive in the second quadrant, so the circle gives a second point at the same height.

Identities: To replace sin²θ or cos²θ, or to turn sin θ/cos θ into tan θ. tan is undefined when cos θ = 0.

3.9.i: A 2 × 2 matrix can move every point in the plane at once. Its columns tell you where the two basic unit vectors land, which determines everything else.
3.9.h: Applying transformations in turn is matrix multiplication, with the first transformation on the right, nearest the point. The determinant measures how area changes; its sign shows whether orientation has been flipped.
3.9.q: Find the image of (2, 1) after a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin, and the area scale factor.
s: With θ = 90°: matrix (0 −1; 1 0).
cos 90° = 0 and sin 90° = 1 in the rotation formula.
Multiply the matrix by the position vector of the point.
det = 0 − (−1) = 1, so area is unchanged.
A rotation does not stretch shapes, which is a useful check.

Rotation: θ the angle turned anticlockwise about the origin.
For rotations about O. For clockwise, use −θ.
Reflection in y = (tan θ)x: θ the angle the mirror line makes with the positive x-axis.
For reflections in lines through the origin. Note the double angle.
Area scale factor: To find an image's area. Take the size of the determinant.

3.10.i: A vector is a journey: how far and in what direction. It doesn't matter where the journey starts, unless it's a position vector, which starts at the origin.
3.10.h: Going from A to B is the same as going from A back to O and then on to B, which gives AB = b − a. Dividing a vector by its length keeps its direction but makes its length exactly 1.
3.10.q: For A(1, 2, 2) and B(3, 3, 4), find AB and a unit vector in its direction.
s: End minus start gives the journey from A to B.
Pythagoras in three directions gives the length.
Unit vector = (2/3, 1/3, 2/3).
Dividing by the magnitude scales the length to 1.

Magnitude: For the length of a vector; in context it may be a distance or a speed.
Displacement: a, b the position vectors of A and B.
For the vector from A to B. It is end minus start.

3.11.i: A vector line equation is a set of directions: start at a point, then travel any amount along a direction. Each value of λ picks out one point.
3.11.h: To test for intersection in 3D, equate the components: three equations in two parameters. Solve two and check the third. If they fail and the directions are not parallel, the lines are skew.
s: x: 1 + λ = 3 gives λ = 2.
The x equation has only one unknown, so start there.
y: λ = 4 + μ gives μ = −2.
Use λ to find the other parameter.
z: 2 = 2, which holds.
The third equation is the test: it must also be true for the lines really to meet.
Substitute λ into its own line to find the position.

Vector equation of a line: r any point on the line, a a known point, b direction vector, λ parameter.
To describe a line in 2D or 3D.
Parametric form: (x₀, y₀, z₀) a point, (l, m, n) the direction, λ parameter.
To work component by component, for intersections or finding a particular point.

3.12.i: Position equals start plus time multiplied by velocity. Each component moves independently, and speed is simply the length of the velocity vector.
3.12.h: Two objects being in the same place at the same time needs the same t in both equations; paths can cross at different times. For closest approach, write the distance between them as a function of t and minimise it.
3.12.q: A ship is at r = (2, 1) + t(3, 4) km after t hours. Find its speed and position after 2 hours.
s: Speed = √(9 + 16) = 5 km/h.
Speed is the size of the velocity vector, with no direction.
Substitute t into the position equation.

Constant velocity: r₀ initial position, v velocity vector, t time.
Speed: Whenever speed, not velocity, is asked for.

3.13.i: The scalar product measures how much two vectors point the same way. The vector product makes a new vector at right angles to both.
3.13.h: From the cosine rule, v·w = |v||w|cos θ, so v·w = 0 means perpendicular. |v × w| = |v||w|sin θ is base × height, the area of the parallelogram; half of it is the triangle's area.
3.13.q: Find the angle between v = (1, 2, 2) and w = (2, 0, 1).
s: Multiply matching components and add.
The formula needs both lengths.
Rearranging the definition of the scalar product isolates the angle.

Scalar product: v₁…, w₁… components, θ the angle between the vectors.
To find angles or test perpendicularity. Vectors must both point away from the angle's vertex.
Vector product magnitude: θ the angle between v and w.
For parallelogram area; halve it for a triangle.
Angle: For the angle between vectors or lines (use direction vectors).

3.14.i: A graph is a set of dots joined by lines, showing what is connected to what. Distances on the page don't matter, only the connections.
3.14.h: Each edge has two ends, so adding all the degrees counts every edge twice. That is why the number of odd-degree vertices must be even. A tree has just enough edges to connect its vertices, so adding any edge creates a cycle.
3.14.q: A simple graph has degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 2. How many edges does it have?
s: Sum of degrees = 12.
The handshaking lemma starts from this total.
Each edge is counted once from each end.

Handshaking lemma: deg(v) degree of a vertex, |E| number of edges.
For any graph, to count edges or show a degree list is impossible.
Edges of K_n: For a complete graph: every pair of vertices is joined once.

3.15.i: An adjacency matrix is the graph stored as a table. Multiplying the table by itself counts routes, because each extra power adds one more step.
3.15.h: To go from i to j in two steps, you go through some middle vertex k; the sum over k of a_ik × a_kj is exactly the (i, j) entry of A². A transition matrix instead divides each column by its total, making probabilities.
3.15.q: A = (0 1; 1 1). How many walks of length 2 go from vertex 2 to vertex 2?
s: A power k of the matrix counts walks with exactly k steps.
Entry (2, 2) of A² is 2.
Row 2, column 2 is the walk from vertex 2 to vertex 2.

Walks of length k: A adjacency matrix, k steps, i start vertex, j end vertex.
To count walks of exactly k steps. Sum powers of A for walks of up to k steps.

3.16.i: These algorithms answer practical network problems: the cheapest way to connect everything, the shortest way to walk every road, and the shortest tour of every town.
3.16.h: Kruskal and Prim are guaranteed to give a minimum spanning tree. For the Chinese postman, odd vertices force repeated edges, so you pair them as cheaply as possible. The travelling salesman has no quick exact method, so bounds trap the answer.
3.16.q: A network has odd vertices A and B only. The total weight of its edges is 90 and the shortest path from A to B is 12. Find the shortest closed route that uses every edge.
s: Two odd vertices means one pairing: A with B.
An Eulerian circuit needs all even degrees, so odd vertices must be joined by repeated edges.
Repeat the shortest route between A and B: 12.
The repeated edges should add as little as possible.
Every edge is walked once, plus the repeated route.
